paras: The lynching of Ben Edwards took place at Amite City, Louisiana, on the night of January 28, 1888, when a body of about 100 armed men took Edwards, a Black man, from the town jail and hanged him to a tree. Edwards had been jailed on the accusation that he had criminally assaulted Catherine Hughes, a white girl who lived near the town. A dispatch from Amite City to the New Orleans Times-Democrat ran in papers from California to South Carolina, often under headlines such as "A Fiend Quickly Disposed Of."

According to the Times-Democrat dispatch as printed in the St. Tammany Farmer of Covington, Louisiana, Edwards was accused of criminally assaulting Miss Catherine Hughes, a white girl living seven miles from Amite City. The condensed wire version placed the assault "on Friday last," January 27, and said the sheriff captured Edwards and lodged him in jail on Saturday night. The fuller text, written on Saturday, said instead that Sheriff Mix had gone in pursuit of Edwards "yesterday," captured him and jailed him. The same dispatch noted that another prisoner, a man named Dranghon, had escaped on the Wednesday night before.

At 10:30 on Saturday night a body of armed men numbering about 100 came into Amite City, unmasked. They arrested the deputy sheriff and compelled him to hand over the jail keys, while Sheriff Mix was away, supposedly searching for Dranghon. The condensed wire, which did not mention the deputy, said the men forced the sheriff himself to give up the keys.

The men took Edwards out, carried him about 100 yards from the jail and hanged him to a tree. After the hanging, the dispatch said, the crowd "quietly dispersed," and none of its members was named in any report.

No report of an inquest, arrest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage. The latest item found, in the Brookhaven Leader of Mississippi on February 9, said only that Edwards had been taken from the jail "recently" and hung, and added that "His crime merited the direst doom."

Most readers learned of the lynching from the Times-Democrat special, which appeared on January 30 in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Indianapolis Journal, the Savannah Morning News, the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer and the Fort Worth Daily Gazette, among others. Headlines treated the accusation as proven: "A Fiend Quickly Disposed Of" in Sacramento, "A Ravisher Lynched" in Savannah, "A Colored Ravisher Lynched" in Unionville, Nevada, and "A Negro Brute Disposed Of" in the Nicodemus Cyclone of Kansas. The Fort Worth Daily Gazette headed the story "Hanged to a Tree" over the line "How a Negro Assaulter was Treated by a Louisiana Mob," while the Indianapolis Journal used "A Woman's Assailant Lynched."

Through early February the story moved through syndicated news-summary columns, cut to a single sentence giving the charge and the lynching. In the condensing the details drifted: several summaries dated the lynching "the 29th," the Daily Republican and the Elko Daily Independent said Friday night, two summaries named the girl "Catherine Haves" or "Hayes," and the Nicodemus Cyclone placed Amite City in Mississippi.

Southern papers near the scene ran short notices, with the Yorkville Enquirer of South Carolina saying Edwards was lynched "for brutally assaulting a white woman." The Southern Herald of Liberty, Mississippi, and the Elko Daily Independent were among the few to describe Edwards as "charged with" the assault rather than guilty of it. Others endorsed the killing outright: the New Ulm Weekly Review of Minnesota called the lynchers "indignant citizens," and the Brookhaven Leader wrote that Edwards's crime "merited the direst doom."

Reports disagree on the date: most put the lynching on Saturday night, January 28, while the Daily Republican and the Elko Daily Independent said Friday night and several weekly summaries said the 29th. The St. Tammany Farmer's text, which timed the hanging at 10:30 on the night the dispatch was written, is the most detailed, and the summaries giving the 29th match the January 29 dateline of the wire. Accounts also differ on whether the sheriff or his deputy surrendered the jail keys, with the fuller dispatch naming the deputy and placing the sheriff elsewhere.

framing.detail: The wire headlines presented the accusation as fact and the lynching as a fitting end: 'A Fiend Quickly Disposed Of', 'A Ravisher Lynched', 'A Negro Brute Disposed Of'.

Most papers ran the Times-Democrat special or a one-line condensation in news-summary columns without comment.
